21.text: I may mention here that Eiˊheli tried to give other information of a

22.text: similar kind, and of no better quality. For instance, he told me that in the

23.text: earlier times the Chukchee were much incensed in cases of adultery. Thus,

24.text: if a married woman were caught with a man, both had their noses cut off by

25.text: way of punishment. The husband would say to his wife, “Your beauty is

26.text: much prized by this fellow. Now see what will be left of it.” This whole

27.text: narration has hardly anything to do with the facts of real life. In reality, a

28.text: Chukchee man, when having caught his wife with another man, will perhaps

29.text: feel angry. Then he will go to the camp of the trespasser, have intercourse

30.text: with his wife, and by this means form with him a tie of group-marriage.²

31.text: In respect to particular cases of acts of violence on very young girls, I know

39.text: ² Of the tribes of northeastern Asia, the Koryak, and partly the Kamchadal, consider adultery as a serious

40.text: trespass. Perhaps the narrative of Eiˊheli refers in some degree to the traditions of these tribes. It is known

41.text: that among several peoples adultery is punished by cutting off the nose of the woman and of her seducer.

42.text: E. Westermarck (History of Human Marriage, p. 122) mentions such a practice as existing among several tribes

43.text: of North America, India, etc. Among others, Clark Wissler (Annual Archæological Report, being the Appendix

44.text: to the Report of the Minister of Education, Ontario, 1905, p. 173) mentions that with the Blackfoot Indians,
